extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of humour theory, philosophy, and psychoanalysis
extracted.subtask_description: The chapter analyzes classical theoretical criteria for humour from Bergson and Freud, offering normative claims about what counts as comedy, the role of language and gesture, and how jokes relate to social repression and the unconscious. It is aimed at guiding theoretical interpretation rather than practical joke-writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy's relation to tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: High-class theatrical comedy does not aspire to heights of tragic drama.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comedy should not be judged by standards appropriate to tragedy; it occupies a different aesthetic aim. Evaluations of comedic quality should consider whether the work pursues its own comic aims rather than aspiring to tragic pathos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comedy situated between art and life
rubrics_metrics.description: Comedy ‘is situated on the border-line between art and life’.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good comedy often draws on everyday social life and ordinary situations. When classifying or analysing a comic work, assess how it negotiates the boundary between realistic social behavior and artistic shaping.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dulling sympathy; gesture over action
rubrics_metrics.description: The comic writer must dull the audience’s sympathy for the character and allow gesture to appear more important than action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Bergsonian criterion: comedic effectiveness can arise from creating a certain emotional distance (reduced sympathy) and foregrounding mechanical or exaggerated gestures rather than dramatic plot-driven action. Anti-pattern: treating comic characters with the intense pathos reserved for tragic protagonists.

rubrics_metrics.name: Visual/gesture primacy in screen comedy
rubrics_metrics.description: By means of close-up shots, film and television can convey a subtlety of gesture ... the gestures and expressions of the characters count for more than the scripted wit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In screen media, evaluate how nonverbal expression (facial expression, micro-gesture) carries comedic meaning; examples given include Curb Your Enthusiasm and The Office (comedies of embarrassment) where audience laughter is often prompted by gesture when wit fails.

rubrics_metrics.name: Skepticism towards verbal humour / language limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Bergson’s theoretical downgrading of verbal humour reflects intuitionism’s search for the reality of constant change behind the appearance of fixity. Language can hinder this search, for it contains fixed categories that seem to take objects for granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing humour, consider Bergson’s warning that verbal jokes, puns and labels may flatten individuality and disguise fleeting inner states. Stronger comedic insights may come from forms that circumvent fixed linguistic categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Art's role in capturing inner realities
rubrics_metrics.description: Only novelists, poets and artists can really capture this inner reality; the fixed terms of everyday language or conventional psychology come nowhere near to doing so.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses of humour should recognise the special capacity of artistic media to represent subtle, transient inner states that ordinary language cannot. Works that rely solely on conventional psychological/linguistic labels may be judged as failing this standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Look behind language to intuition
rubrics_metrics.description: The distrust of language appears as a theme in Laughter: 'we do not see things themselves but ... we confine ourselves to reading the labels affixed to them'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A Bergsonian analytic move: seek the non-linguistic realities (intuition, feeling, gesture) behind surface labels. When critiquing comic material, probe whether the humour exposes or merely repeats everyday labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laughter as social act / disciplinary function
rubrics_metrics.description: Bergson affirms the need to place laughter in its social context ... the action of laughing is itself a social act. Having asserted that laughter in general plays a necessary, disciplinary function ...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate humour not only as individual reaction but as social practice that can enforce norms, discipline behavior, or mark deviation. Analyses should examine how laughter operates within group interactions and what social work it performs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include the act of laughing in analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: The analysis of laughter is not confined to identifying the objects of humour. As Bergson stressed, the action of laughing is itself a social act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not restrict critique to the content that is laughed at; include the performative, interactive and situational dimensions of laughter (who laughs, when, and to what social effect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Freudian claim: jokes conceal unconscious content
rubrics_metrics.description: The joke is seldom ‘just’ a joke, but it hides secrets even more discreditable than Hobbes ever imagined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adopt a hermeneutic stance that searches for concealed motivations or wishes beneath the apparent surface of jokes. Treat jokes as potential evidence of repressed material rather than purely innocuous entertainment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jokes as social mechanisms for pleasure
rubrics_metrics.description: According to Freud, a joke is ‘the most social of all the mental functions that aim at a yield of pleasure’.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating jokes, address both their pleasure-yielding function and their social distribution: jokes produce shared pleasure and operate within social contexts—assess how social dynamics shape who benefits from the joke.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply dream-work decoding to jokes
rubrics_metrics.description: Unconscious desires disguise themselves ... the dream-work ensures that the underlying desire is 'translated', often through complex processes of condensation and substitution. Similar processes are at work with jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use Freudian analytic tools (condensation, displacement/substitution) to decode jokes: look for symbolic condensations and substitutions that disguise latent wishful meanings in manifest comic content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assume non-innocence of jokes (wish-fulfilment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Freud maintained there are 'no “innocent” dreams' and argued for the ubiquity of wish-fulfilment; by extension, jokes too are seldom innocent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate purportedly innocent or casual jokes skeptically—consider whether they function as expressions of wish-fulfilment or disguised gratification of impulses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repression and jokes as expressions of repressed instincts
rubrics_metrics.description: Freud's theory depicts repression as the means by which unruly human nature is socially disciplined. The unconscious rebels against this discipline in dreams, slips of the tongue and jokes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In analyses, situate jokes as outlets or symptoms of repressed sexual/aggressive instincts. Consider jokes' role in discharging or masking libidinal/aggressive energy in socially permissible forms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include social/parental mechanisms in analysis (critique of Freud)
rubrics_metrics.description: Freud becomes somewhat unsociological when describing how repression occurs ... he tended to presume that the psychological imperatives come from within the individual child, overlooking how parents exert discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A comprehensive rubric for analysing humour should not only probe intrapsychic processes but also investigate concrete socialization practices (parental discipline, social rituals) that produce repression and shape humour. Avoid an analysis that treats repression as purely internal and ahistorical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Synthesis: combine disciplinary and unconscious perspectives
rubrics_metrics.description: Bergson’s disciplinary analysis of laughter can be combined with Freud’s idea that laughter has its own secrets ... such a combination points the way toward a critique of ideological positivism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When theorising or critiquing humour, integrate macro-social (disciplinary, normative) accounts with micro-psychological (unconscious, wishful) readings. Use both perspectives to reveal how humour polices social norms while also concealing desires.

rubrics_metrics.name: Culturally situated examples matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Freud collected and used Jewish anecdotes and jokes, often to make a serious point: 'It was as if he brought the joke forward as an example of how wisdom is expressed in wit'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyses should attend to the cultural provenance of jokes; culturally specific material can embody communal wisdom or particular unconscious themes. Avoid treating jokes as decontextualised units.
